plan.title: Paired 3-condition blood RNA-seq: treated_a/treated_b vs control
plan.analytical_narrative:
The data are 12,000 gene-symbol rows x 12 blood RNA-seq libraries (Salmon raw counts, counts.csv) from 4 subjects, each contributing one control, one treated_a and one treated_b sample (metadata.csv: sample, subject, condition), single batch. The design is a complete randomized-block: subject is a nuisance factor with 4 levels, condition the factor of interest with 3 levels. The only correct analysis is a paired/blocked model — ~ subject + condition — which absorbs between-subject expression variation and leaves 12 - 4 - 2 = 6 residual degrees of freedom. Ignoring the subject block would waste most of the power in a 4-subject study; treating subject as random is unnecessary here because the design is balanced and every subject sees every condition, so fixed-effect blocking is exact.

Step T1S1 builds the analysis objects: joins counts.csv to metadata.csv, verifies the 4x3 balance and that subject/condition are estimable together, filters low-count genes with edgeR::filterByExpr on the ~ subject + condition design, and produces a VST/log-CPM matrix plus PCA/correlation diagnostics before and after removing subject means. That diagnostic decides nothing statistically but shows whether subject dominates the variance (expected in blood) and whether any sample is an outlier or a mislabelled subject — a real risk in paired designs, where one swapped label destroys the pairing.

Step T1S2 runs the DE model itself in DESeq2 with design ~ subject + condition, control as the reference level, and extracts the three contrasts the question asks for: treated_a vs control, treated_b vs control, and treated_b vs treated_a (the direct treatment-vs-treatment contrast, taken from the same fitted model rather than from a separate two-group refit, so the shrunken dispersions and the subject block are shared). It also runs the omnibus likelihood-ratio test of ~ subject + condition vs ~ subject, which answers 'responds to either treatment' as a single test with one FDR correction instead of a union of two thresholded lists. With n=4 per condition, dispersion estimation is thin; the step must report the number of genes passing filter, the dispersion fit, and independent-filtering behaviour, and must use apeglm/ashr shrunken LFCs for ranking rather than raw MLE fold changes.

Step T1S3 reconciles the three contrasts: which genes are shared responders (significant in both treatment-vs-control contrasts and concordant in sign), which are private to one treatment, and — critically — which of the apparently 'private' genes actually have a significant treated_b vs treated_a difference. A gene significant in one arm and not the other is not evidence of a treatment difference; only the direct contrast tests that. This step enforces that distinction explicitly and produces the effect-size scatter and per-subject count plots that let a reader judge whether a hit is driven by one subject.

Step T2S1 takes the three ranked gene lists into fgsea against the staged human MSigDB hallmark and GO:BP collections plus human WikiPathways, using the shrunken-LFC ranking rather than a cut list, because at n=4 the significant-gene lists may be too short for over-representation testing to have any power. It reports which pathways move under either treatment and which differ between them.

The question mentions treatments but supplies no PK, safety, outcome or compound data, so no translational, PK/PD or safety steps are warranted; adding them would be speculation.
